_description: Every pop-up window, by id. Map '!' markers, HUD buttons and the flow open pop-ups by these ids. Each pop-up: 'title', 'body' (a list of blocks, shown top to bottom), optional 'button' (label of the closing button; default from ui.json). Block types: {"type":"text","text":...} a paragraph; {"type":"stat","value":"5M gal","label":...} a big number; {"type":"citation","text":...,"url":optional} a source line; {"type":"chat","with":{"name":"Ruth","character":0},"lines":[{"from":"alex"|"them","text":...}]} a conversation: Alex's face on the left, theirs on the right (character 0 = farmer, 1 = council member), messages appearing one at a time (used by people you talk to); {"type":"image","illustration":"valley-home","caption":optional} a built-in picture (same names as the intro slides); {"type":"bill","items":[{"label":"Electricity","before":95,"after":160}],"totalLabel":"You now owe","total":optional (default = sum of the increases),"currency":"$","beforeLabel","afterLabel","note"} a bill with increases in red; {"type":"audioPlayer","sound":"datacenter","label":...,"autoplay":true|false} play/pause and volume for a sound in audio.json; {"type":"keys","rows":[{"keys":["W","A"],"label":...}]} keyboard keys with what they do (write "↑", "↓", "←", "→" for arrow keys; they are drawn as arrows).
_usedIn: Simulation page → pop-ups over the game (controls, '!' markers, later HUD buttons)

controls._location: Shown over the valley right after '6 months later'
controls.title: How to play

body.text: Walk Alex around Datadew Valley. Look for the ! markers and read what changed after the data center arrived.

rows.label: Or walk with the arrow keys
Read a ! when you are next to it

body.text: This experience uses sound. Headphones are recommended.

river-contamination._location: Valley: the river and the well on its bank (they glow when Alex is near); '!' beside Alex's side of the river
river-contamination.title: The river

body.text: Since the data center opened, the river has become noticeably murkier. Data center construction can send muddy runoff into nearby waterways, while some cooling systems produce wastewater containing concentrated salts and chemicals that can cause harmful water quality.
Community members have always relied on the well for drinking water. Now they are worried about contamination from wastewater.
Gour et al., 2026

bills._location: Valley: Alex's mailbox (the red '-$'), in front of the cottage
bills.title: This month's bills

body.text: Electricity and water bills keep climbing as nearby data centers place growing demands on local resources. Data centers accounted for nearly 4% of U.S. electricity demand in 2023, and their cooling systems can strain local water supplies.
Chen et al., 2026

air-quality-smog._location: Valley: '!' east of the data center, in the smog
air-quality-smog.title: The air

body.text: Data centers contribute both carbon emissions and environmental pollutants, causing detrimental effects on human health. Emissions primarily come from the construction, infrastructure and hardware manufacturing of the data center systems. Emissions from backup generators and power plants can contribute to respiratory and cardiovascular diseases in individuals located near the data centers.
George, 2026
Gupta et al., 2021

individual-health._location: HUD: clicking Alex's portrait or name (top-left)
individual-health.title: How Alex feels

body.text: Living near the data center has had immense effects on Alex’s health. He has developed an ongoing cough and has disrupted sleep from the ongoing hum from the data center. Additionally financial stress has caused Alex to fall into mental detriment.
George, 2026
Martin and Peskoe, 2025

noise-pollution._location: HUD: clicking the speaker button (bottom-left); the recording starts playing
noise-pollution.title: The sound of a data center

body.label: Listen: what it sounds like next to a data center

body.text: The noise of a data center often sounds like a high pitched hum, overpowering other sound frequencies and causing immense distress to those who live nearby. This noise can negatively contribute to the well-being of health, increasing cardiovascular risk and cognitive functioning.
Grumke, 2026

cooling-water-usage._location: Inside the data center: '!' on the municipal water tank
cooling-water-usage.title: Water for cooling

body.text: Almost all the electricity used from data centers turns into heat. Many data centers use cooling towers that evaporate freshwater to release this heat, consuming thousands of liters of water every hour.
In 2023, one major technology company’s data centers alone consumed over 23 billion liters of freshwater for cooling, nearly 80% of which was clean enough to drink.
Li et al., 2025

electricity-usage._location: Inside the data center: '!' on the power cabinets
electricity-usage.title: The power it takes

body.text: Servers and coolers account for the majority of energy consumption by data centers, followed by storage drives and network devices. These systems run 24/7 and thus their energy use is immense. With growing use of this infrastructure comes increased demand for energy and more strain on people like Alex.
O’Donnell and Crownhart, 2025
Masanet and Lei, 2020
